```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rPSTool)
# Result columns are named by what they hold, e.g. "ac_a_rw25_wl_c" (Angular Choice, angular distance, walking radius 25,
# length-weighted, syntax-normalised). `pick()` selects a column by a pattern on that name instead of by position.
pick <- function(x, pattern) {
  hit <- grep(pattern, names(x))
  stopifnot(length(hit) == 1L)
  x[[hit]]
}
```

This vignette describes what the PST engine can do, which part of that rPSTool
exposes, how that relates to PST for QGIS, and what is not supported. For a first analysis on real data see
`vignette("getting-started", package = "rPSTool")`.

Links to `docs/...` files point to the rPSTool source repository,
<https://github.com/kimonkrenz/rPSTool/tree/main/docs>.

## 1. What is PST, and what is rPSTool?

Three pieces are easy to confuse.

* **The PST engine** is a C++ library (`pstalgo`) from the *Place Syntax Tool*
  project. It contains the algorithms: graph construction, shortest paths,
  depth, weighting, radii and the native normalisation formulas.
* **PST for QGIS** is a Python plugin that uses the engine. It decides which
  engine function a menu entry calls, which arrays are passed, which defaults
  the dialogs offer, and how results are written back to a QGIS layer.
* **rPSTool** is an R interface to the same engine. It compiles a pinned copy of
  the original engine (PST v3.3.2, commit
  `63df80a2cf3dd289be95ea3d91667c3490719b75`) into the package. Installing it
  needs neither QGIS, Python, nor a separate PST installation, and nothing is
  downloaded at run time.

rPSTool does not reimplement the PST algorithms; its analytical values come from
the engine. The QGIS plugin is used as the reference for *how the original
application drives the engine*; it does not limit what R users can ask the
engine to do.

## 2. Validation status

rPSTool calls the same pinned engine as PST for QGIS. The inputs and defaults of the plugin were read from its source.
Results have not been compared with real runs inside QGIS; the manual procedure is in
[`tools/validation/qgis-comparison/`](https://github.com/kimonkrenz/rPSTool/tree/main/tools/validation/qgis-comparison).
No numerical equivalence with PST for QGIS is claimed: the statements below mean that the same engine is called with equivalent
arguments. The engine computes in single precision (`float`). Values the plugin derives on the Python side (for example mean
depth or area unit conversion) are not engine outputs.

## 3. Graph families

PST has distinct native graph types, and each analysis needs one of them. A
graph is built once, lives in native memory, and can be reused by any number of
analyses.

| Graph (constructor) | Analyses that use it |
|---|---|
| Axial graph, `axial_graph()` (lines that cross; optional unlinks, points and polygon point groups) | `network_integration()`, `network_reach()`, `network_betweenness()` (including attraction points), `attraction_reach()`, `attraction_distance()`, `od_betweenness()`; inspection with `axial_line_lengths()` and `axial_crossing_coords()` |
| Segment graph, `segment_graph()` (lines connected at endpoints) | `angular_integration()`, `angular_choice()`, `segment_grouping()` |
| Segment-group graph, `segment_group_graph()` (built from a segment graph and group assignments) | `segment_group_integration()` |
| No graph | `create_segment_map()`, `create_junctions()` (construction from coordinates); `isovist_context()` and `isovist()`; `compare_line_results()`, `raster_data()`, `raster_to_polygons()` |

The engine's graph types are not interchangeable (family boundaries are
described in `docs/compatibility/core-network-analyses.md`). The example uses a
small axial map and a segment map:

```{r graphs}
lines <- rbind(c(0, 0, 60, 0), c(10, -20, 10, 30), c(30, -5, 30, 18),
               c(30, 12, 70, 12), c(55, -10, 55, 10), c(70, 12, 70, 40),
               c(-10, 25, 25, 25))
g <- axial_graph(lines)

segments <- rbind(c(0, 0, 10, 0), c(10, 0, 18, 6), c(18, 6, 18, 16),
                  c(18, 6, 30, 9), c(10, 0, 10, -8), c(30, 9, 36, 20))
sg <- segment_graph(segments)

network_integration(g, radius = analysis_radius(steps = 2))
```

## 4. Capability map

The tables show which analyses PST for QGIS offers, which rPSTool exposes, and where they differ.

### 4.1 Available in both PST for QGIS and rPSTool

| Analysis | rPSTool | Differences and limits |
|---|---|---|
| Network Integration | `network_integration()` | Like the QGIS dialog, rPSTool accepts only a steps radius (or none); other radius limits are rejected before the native call. rPSTool returns the node count and total depth; the plugin's mean-depth column is a Python-side value. |
| Network Integration, junction scores | `network_integration(junctions = TRUE)` | The plugin's code for this feature references undefined names, so it fails in QGIS (from the plugin source; not run in QGIS). |
| Reach | `network_reach()` | Native area in squared coordinate units; the QGIS area-unit option is a Python rescaling. Supplied origin points are accepted. |
| Segment Betweenness | `network_betweenness()` | Unnormalised and standard-normalised results are the common subset (see 4.2 for the rest). |
| Attraction Betweenness | `network_betweenness(attraction_points = )` | |
| Angular Integration | `angular_integration()` | See section 6 for normalisation. |
| Angular Choice | `angular_choice()` | See section 6 for angle settings and normalisation. |
| Attraction Reach | `attraction_reach()` | Default decay differs (section 7). |
| Attraction Distance | `attraction_distance()` | |
| OD Betweenness | `od_betweenness()` | |
| Create Segment Map | `create_segment_map()` | Different default for `extrude` (section 7). |
| Create Junctions | `create_junctions()` | |
| Compare Results (normalised mode) | `compare_line_results()`, `raster_data()`, `raster_to_polygons()` | |
| Graph services (axial and segment graph, line lengths, crossing coordinates) | `axial_graph()`, `segment_graph()`, `axial_line_lengths()`, `axial_crossing_coords()` | |

### 4.2 Provided by the engine and exposed by rPSTool, restricted or not offered in PST for QGIS

| Capability | How PST for QGIS restricts it |
|---|---|
| Several radius limits in one run (Reach, Network and Attraction Betweenness, OD Betweenness, Attraction Reach) | the plugin splits the ticked radius types into separate runs |
| Walking, straight, angular or axmeter radius for Network Integration | steps radius only; rPSTool follows this and rejects other radii |
| Network Betweenness with angular distance | the wizard offers walking, steps and axmeter |
| Freeman and syntax normalisation of Segment Betweenness | never called by the plugin |
| Unrestricted Reach and Betweenness (empty `analysis_radius()`) | with no limit ticked nothing is computed |
| OD Betweenness with a `steps` radius | the wizard offers straight, walking and angular radii |
| Diagnostic outputs (node count, total depth, total depth weight, total weight) always returned | written only for the options a user ticks |
| Attraction Distance destination indices | read internally, never written |
| Segment Grouping and Segment Group Integration | not reachable from the plugin menus (from the plugin source; not run in QGIS) |
| Isovist (context, field of view, direction, perimeter, visible objects, area) | wizard commented out and map tools disabled in the plugin |
| Compare Results in relative-percent mode | the plugin hard-codes the normalised mode |
| Graph-retained points and polygon point groups as origins and OD destinations, indexed line input, unlinks on graph and junction creation | QGIS builds points per analysis |

Multi-radius and multi-normalisation calls (section 8) are a convenience of
rPSTool for the two angular analyses: each radius runs the engine once.

### 4.3 Not supported

| Item | Why it is not supported | Behaviour of rPSTool |
|---|---|---|
| Fast Segment Betweenness (the plugin's "Angular Betweenness") | experimental engine routine whose header, implementation and upstream tests disagree; its results differ from Angular Choice | not exposed |
| Visual Connectivity | the engine function validates its descriptor and returns without computing | not exposed |
| `axmeter` radius in Angular Integration and Choice | the engine's angular radius setup does not read it; the plugin result with an axmeter radius equals the unrestricted result | rejected with an error |
| `axmeter` radius in OD Betweenness | the engine never reads it | rejected with an error |
| `axmeter` in Attraction Distance | not supported by the engine | rejected |
| Segment Group Integration with straight, angular or axmeter radii | only walking and steps are supported | rejected |
| Segment Betweenness with `straight` or `weights` distance | the engine accepts walking, steps, angular and axmeter only | rejected |
| Attraction Distance, straight-only, point-group origins | PST never writes the group outputs on that path | rejected |
| Segment graphs with more than 32 segments at one coordinate | the engine does not support them and returns a wrong node count | rejected |
| Segment-map detail reduction that would close a segment onto its own start | PST would crash or return a zero-length self-loop (`docs/compatibility/network-construction.md`) | rejected |
| Split Polylines | uses only QGIS geometry code, not a PST engine function | not applicable |

There is no API for user-defined progress callbacks, for cancellation, or for PST's native log callback; see `docs/progress.md`.

## 5. Radius semantics

`analysis_radius()` holds up to five independent limits, each `NULL`
(unrestricted) or a finite non-negative number.

* **Units.** `straight` and `walking` are in the coordinate units of the
  input, `angular` in degrees, and `steps` is a whole number of topological
  steps. No unit conversion is performed. `axmeter` is the engine's
  accumulated length with topological weighting, not another spelling for
  walking.
* **Combination.** All limits you supply apply together in a single run, so a
  line is reached only if the traversal satisfies every one of them (an AND).
  The engine's own traversal semantics are preserved; for some combinations,
  for example a finite straight limit together with others, see the per-family
  notes in `docs/compatibility/`.
* **Multi-radius.** One field may hold several values, for example
  `analysis_radius(walking = c(20, 30))`, and then the analysis runs once per
  value, with the other fields as fixed restrictions. There is no Cartesian
  product. Only `angular_choice()` and `angular_integration()` accept this; all
  other analyses reject it.
* **`axmeter`.** Accepted by the axial analyses that use it; rejected by the
  angular analyses and OD Betweenness (section 4.3).

How PST for QGIS combines limits depends on the analysis (see
`docs/compatibility/qgis-differences.md`). It runs one analysis per ticked
limit type for Reach, Network Betweenness, Attraction Betweenness, OD
Betweenness, Segment Group Integration and Attraction Reach. It does not split
Angular Integration and Angular Choice (one combined radius), and Network
Integration offers a steps radius only. rPSTool always combines. To mimic the
splitting analyses, call once per limit. To see that combining matters, choose
limits where each alone and both together give different results:

```{r radius}
rad_steps    <- analysis_radius(steps = 2)
rad_walking  <- analysis_radius(walking = 55)
rad_combined <- analysis_radius(steps = 2, walking = 55)
reach <- cbind(
  steps_only   = pick(network_reach(g, radius = rad_steps), "^rc_"),
  walking_only = pick(network_reach(g, radius = rad_walking), "^rc_"),
  combined     = pick(network_reach(g, radius = rad_combined), "^rc_"))
reach
# lines whose combined count differs from the steps-only / the walking-only count
c(vs_steps = sum(reach[, "combined"] != reach[, "steps_only"]),
  vs_walking = sum(reach[, "combined"] != reach[, "walking_only"]))
```

## 6. Weighting, normalisation and angle settings

Normalisation is applied by the engine's exported normalisation routines;
rPSTool does not use R formulas for it. Angular Choice offers `"none"`,
`"standard"`, `"turner"` and `"syntax"`; Angular Integration offers its own set
(`"turner"` (default), `"syntax"` and `"hillier"`);
Network Betweenness offers `"none"`, `"standard"`, `"freeman"` and `"syntax"`.

In its length-weighted Angular Choice run the plugin divides by the
length-weighted total depth for the syntax (NACH) normalisation, and in its
unweighted run by the plain total depth (see
`docs/compatibility/qgis-differences.md`). rPSTool makes
the same pairing and passes the length-weighted total depth (`tdw_..._wl`) when
`weigh_by_length = TRUE` and the total depth (`td_...`) otherwise.

The chunk below is a **check**, not how rPSTool computes the values. The engine's
exported syntax normaliser for Angular Choice is
`log10(choice + 1) / log10(2 + TD)`, and the
code recomputes it in R from the returned columns to confirm the pairing:

```{r choice-weighted}
w  <- angular_choice(sg, radius = analysis_radius(walking = 25),
                         weigh_by_length = TRUE, normalization = "syntax")
u  <- angular_choice(sg, radius = analysis_radius(walking = 25),
                         weigh_by_length = FALSE, normalization = "syntax")
all.equal(pick(w, "^ac_.*_c$"), log10(pick(w, "^ac_.*_n$") + 1) / log10(2 + pick(w, "^tdw_")),
          tolerance = 1e-6)
all.equal(pick(u, "^ac_.*_c$"), log10(pick(u, "^ac_.*_n$") + 1) / log10(2 + pick(u, "^td_")),
          tolerance = 1e-6)
```

### Angle threshold and precision

Turns smaller than `angle_threshold` degrees count as zero, and
`angle_precision` sets the rounding unit used when ranking paths. These change
depths and therefore normalised values:

```{r angles}
chain <- structure(c(7.9, 20.6, 30.5, 37.5, 50, 57, 30.5, 6, 7.7, 11.6,
  11.2, 12.8, 10.6, 11.6, 20.6, 30.5, 37.5, 50, 57, 68.3, 40.9, 7.7, 11.6,
  11.2, 12.8, 10.6, 4.6, 24.1), dim = c(7L, 4L))
bent <- segment_graph(chain)
a0  <- angular_choice(bent, normalization = "syntax",
                          angle_threshold = 0,  angle_precision = 1)
a15 <- angular_choice(bent, normalization = "syntax",
                          angle_threshold = 15, angle_precision = 1)
round(rbind(threshold_0 = pick(a0, "^ac_.*_c$"), threshold_15 = pick(a15, "^ac_.*_c_at15$")), 2)
```

rPSTool applies explicitly supplied angle settings in both the weighted and the
unweighted run. In the pinned plugin the unweighted Angular Choice branch does
not forward them to the engine, so the engine defaults (threshold 0,
precision 1) apply there; rPSTool does not copy this. To obtain the number
that plugin run would have produced, pass the defaults explicitly:

```{r qgis-unweighted}
plugin_like <- angular_choice(bent, weigh_by_length = FALSE,
                              normalization = "syntax",
                              angle_threshold = 0, angle_precision = 1)
# identical to not supplying any angle settings, i.e. the engine defaults:
identical(plugin_like, angular_choice(bent, weigh_by_length = FALSE,
                                      normalization = "syntax"))
```

## 7. Intentional differences from PST for QGIS

Main differences from PST for QGIS; the full list is in
`docs/compatibility/qgis-differences.md`:

* **`extrude` in Create Segment Map.** The plugin always passes the snap
  distance; the engine default, and rPSTool's, is 0. Pass `extrude = snap` to
  reproduce the plugin.
* **Attraction Reach decay.** In rPSTool `decay_constant = NULL` means 0 for
  `decay = "constant"` and 1 for `"power"`, `"curve"` and `"divide"`, matching
  the wizard's constant `C = 1` for a nonconstant function. The first decay
  function is spelled `decay = "power"` in rPSTool and `pow` in the QGIS wizard. The **default decay function differs as well**: the wizard
  defaults to `pow`, rPSTool to `"constant"`, so state `decay =` explicitly to
  reproduce the wizard. An explicit `decay_constant`, including 0, is passed
  unchanged.
* **Unweighted Angular Choice angle settings**, discussed in section 6.
* **Polygon attractions with holes.** The plugin reads only the outer ring;
  rPSTool keeps all rings.
* **Reach area** and **mean depth** are Python-side values in the plugin and
  are not produced; they are one-line computations on returned columns.
* **Validation.** Non-finite numbers, invalid angle precision, unsupported radius
  types, malformed geometry and known geographic CRS give an error, where the
  plugin silently skips features.

```{r segmap}
streets <- rbind(c(0, 0), c(40, 0), c(20, 0.7), c(20, 40), c(0, 20), c(40, 20))
rpst_default <- create_segment_map(streets, sections = c(2, 2, 2),
                                   snap = 1, tail = 0, deviation = 0)
plugin_like  <- create_segment_map(streets, sections = c(2, 2, 2),
                                   snap = 1, tail = 0, deviation = 0,
                                   extrude = 1)  # extrude = snap, as in the plugin
c(extrude_0 = nrow(rpst_default$segments), extrude_snap = nrow(plugin_like$segments))
```

The decay chunk compares the three non-constant decay functions with the
documented default constant (1) and with another constant, on a small synthetic
case. It shows that the default is the same as `decay_constant = 1` and that a
different constant changes the result:

```{r decay}
attractions <- rbind(c(2, 2), c(65, 20))
r <- analysis_radius(walking = 70)
decay_check <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("power", "curve", "divide"), function(d) {
  default <- attraction_reach(g, attractions, r, distance = "walking", decay = d)
  c1 <- attraction_reach(g, attractions, r, distance = "walking", decay = d,
                         decay_constant = 1)
  c2 <- attraction_reach(g, attractions, r, distance = "walking", decay = d,
                         decay_constant = 2)
  data.frame(decay = d, default_equals_C1 = identical(default, c1),
             C2_differs_from_C1 = !identical(c1, c2),
             mean_default = round(mean(pick(default, "^ar_")), 4),
             mean_C2 = round(mean(pick(c2, "^ar_")), 4))
}))
decay_check
```

### Geometry

Compare results only after confirming that the same geometry is submitted to
PST. The following is documented in `docs/spatial-io/sf-adapters.md`: the
adapters for axial and segment line input, graph points and attraction points
reject multipart geometry; polygon point groups accept POLYGON and reject
MULTIPOLYGON. `create_segment_map()` is different: with sf input, each part of
a MULTILINESTRING becomes a separate section and no edge connects separate
parts. Polygon attractions keep all rings. rPSTool does not reproject geometry,
and known geographic coordinate reference systems are rejected.

## 8. Reusing graphs and file-based workflows

The graph persists in native memory, so repeated analyses reuse it instead of rebuilding it:

```{r reuse}
radii <- list(steps_2 = analysis_radius(steps = 2), steps_3 = analysis_radius(steps = 3),
              unrestricted = analysis_radius())
vapply(radii, function(r) mean(pick(network_integration(g, radius = r), "^ni_")),
       numeric(1))
```

The angular analyses accept several radii and several normalisations in one
call, running the engine once per radius:

```{r extras}
multi <- angular_choice(sg, radius = analysis_radius(walking = c(20, 30)),
                            normalization = c("standard", "syntax"))
names(multi)
```

A graph can be built directly from a GeoParquet or FlatGeobuf path and
results written to a Parquet file without building R vectors. This needs the optional packages `arrow` (>= 25.0.0, the
version declared in `DESCRIPTION`) and, for the file input, `sf`. The
chunk runs only where a suitable `arrow` is installed:

```{r file, eval = requireNamespace("arrow", quietly = TRUE) && utils::packageVersion("arrow") >= "25.0.0"}
out <- tempfile(fileext = ".parquet")
res <- network_integration(g, radius = analysis_radius(steps = 2), output_file = out)
class(res)
unlink(out)
```

## 9. Other limits

* The engine is an in-memory graph engine. Very deep Angular Choice
  computations on some platforms can exhaust a thread stack and crash the R
  session; see `?angular_choice`.
* Finite straight-radius Reach applies decay at the radius, as PST does
  (`docs/compatibility/attractions.md`).
* Results are data frames in native row order. Analytical columns are the
  engine's single-precision values widened to double.
